# PSTAT 134 vs. non-PSTAT134

## Loading Data and Defining the ML Areas

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(knitr)

background <- read_csv(here('data', 'raw', 'background-clean.csv'))
interest   <- read_csv(here('data', 'raw', 'interest-clean.csv'))
joined     <- inner_join(background, interest, by = 'response_id')

ml_areas <- c(
  "Analysis or classification of images",
  "Deep learning and neural networks",
  "Data acquisition and engineering",
  "Natural language processing and analysis of text",
  "Predictive modeling, generally",
  "Statistical models and inference, generally"
)

```

We chose these six areas because they were the most closely related to machine learning. Students were able to select from eleven areas of interest, and most of them can be argued to connect to ML in some way. However, this selection focuses primarily on areas involving building, training, or applying predictive models, or preparing the data those models rely on. We recognize that this choice of slection is somewhat subjective and that a different selection could lead to slightly different results.

## PSTAT 134 Enrollment

Something we can look at first is how many students in our sample have taken PSTAT 134 compared to those who have not. This tells us how large each group is before we compare their maching learning interests.

```{r}
q134 <- joined |>
  mutate(group_134 = if_else(str_detect(courses, fixed('PSTAT 134')),
                             'Took PSTAT 134', 'Did not take PSTAT 134'))

q134 |>
  count(group_134, name = 'n_students') |>
  mutate(proportion = n_students / sum(n_students)) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = 'Students by PSTAT 134 enrollment')

```

From this table, we can see that PSTAT 134 (Statistical Data Science) is not a commonly taken course among the students in our sample. Only 13 of the 49 respondents (26.5%) reported taking PSTAT 134, while 36 (73.5%) had not. This is a sharp contrast with PSTAT 131, which 44 of the 49 students (89.8%) had taken. Since PSTAT 131 is a prerequisite for PSTAT 134, most students have completed the introductory machine learning course but relatively few continued on to 134, leading to a unbalanced comparison.

## Measuring ML Interest for Each Student

Each student could select any number of the eleven interest areas, so we need a single measure of how interested each student is in machine learning. To do this, we can check which of our six ML areas each student selected and count them, giving every student an ML interest score from 0 to 6. This allows us to compare both groups on the scale!

```{r}
area_long_134 <- q134 |>
  crossing(area = ml_areas) |>
  mutate(selected = str_detect(areas, fixed(area)))

ml_data_134 <- area_long_134 |>
  group_by(response_id, group_134) |>
  summarise(n_ml_areas = sum(selected), .groups = 'drop')

head(ml_data_134)

ml_data_134 |>
  count(group_134, n_ml_areas) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = n_ml_areas, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  kable(caption = 'Number of students by ML areas selected (out of 6)')
```

### Summary

```{r}
ml_data_134 |>
  group_by(group_134) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_ml_areas = mean(n_ml_areas),
            median_ml_areas = median(n_ml_areas),
            min = min(n_ml_areas),
            max = max(n_ml_areas)) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = 'Number of ML-related areas selected, by PSTAT 134 enrollment')
  
```

Students who did not take PSTAT 134 selected slightly more ML related areas on average (4.00) than those who took PSTAT 134 (3.85), although both groups share the same median of 4. Something to note is that students who did not take PSTAT 134 also had a wider range (1 to 6 areas) than those who took it to (2 to 5 areas), likely because that group is nearly three times larger. In all, we can see that the two groups show very similar levels of ML interest, suggesting that taking PSTAT 134 is not really associated with selecting more ML related areas.

## Distribution of ML Interest by Group

While the summary table gives us averages, it does not show how the scores are spread out within each group. A boxplot lets us compare the middle and range of ML interest scores side by side, and adding the individual points shows each student, which is especially helpful since the PSTAT 134 group only has 13 students.

```{r}
ggplot(ml_data_134, aes(x = group_134, y = n_ml_areas, fill = group_134)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0.1, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Number of ML related area selected, by PSTAT 134 enrollment",
       x = NULL, y = 'Number of ML areas (out of 6)') +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = 'none')

```

The boxplots for both groups look nearly identical: each has a median of 4 ML areas, and the middle 50% of students in both groups selected between 3 and 5 areas. The main difference is in the range, since students who did not take PSTAT 134 spread from 1 to 6 areas, while those who took PSTAT 134 stayed between 2 and 5. Overall, the plot supports our summary table, showing that the two groups have very similar distributions of ML interest.

## ML Interest by Area

So far we have only looked at the total number of ML areas each student selected, which can hide differences in which areas each group prefers. Next, we can break the interest down by individual area and compare the proportion of students in each group who selected it. This shows whether students who took PSTAT 134 lean toward certain ML topics more than others.

```{r}
area_props_134 <- area_long_134 |>
  group_by(group_134, area) |>
  summarise(n_selected = sum(selected),
            n_students = n(),
            proportion = n_selected / n_students,
            .groups = 'drop')

area_props_134 |>
  select(area, group_134, proportion) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = group_134, values_from = proportion) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = 'Proportion of students selecting each ML area, by PSTAT 134 enrollment')

ggplot(area_props_134, aes(x = area, y = proportion, fill = group_134)) +
  geom_col(position = 'dodge') +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = 'ML-related interests by PSTAT 134 enrollment',
       x = NULL, y = 'Proportion of students in group', fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1))
```
When we broke the ML interest down by area, some differences show up that the overall totals didnt catch initially. Students who took PSTAT 134 were a lot more into data acquisition and engineering (76.9% vs. 52.8%) and a little into deep learning (84.6% vs. 77.8%). On the other other hand, they picked statistical inference (46.2% vs. 69.4%). image analysis (46.2 % vs. 58.3%), and NLP (46.2% vs. 52.8%) less often. Predictive modeling was the top pick for both groups, with around 88.9% of non-134 students and 84/6% of 134 students choosing it. From this we can say that PSTAT 134 students might lean more toward data engineering and away from traditional stats, but since there are only 13 of them, these differences could just be a random chance.

## Testing for Differences

The tables and plots show some difference between the two groups, but with only 13 students in the PSTAT 134 group, we should check whether these gaps are actually meaningful or could just be random noise. To check, we use Fisher's exact test for each area, since it works well with small groups, and a Wilcox on rank-sum test to compare the total number of ML areas picked, since those scores are counts rahter than normally distributed values.

```{r}
# Fisher's exact test

area_long_134 |>
  group_by(area) |>
  summarise(took_134 = mean(selected[group_134 == 'Took PSTAT 134']),
            not_134 = mean(selected[group_134 == 'Did not take PSTAT 134']),
            p_value = fisher.test(table(group_134, selected))$p.value) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Fisher's exact test by ML area")

# Wiclxo rank sum test
wilcox.test(n_ml_areas ~ group_134, 
            data = ml_data_134, 
            exact = FALSE)

```
From the Fisher's test, it seems like none of the six ML areas showed a statistically significant difference between the two groups, since every p value was well above 0.05. Even with the biggest gaps, like data engineering (p = 0.191) and statistical inference (p = 0.184), were not strong enough to rule out random chance. Additionally, the Wilcox rank sum test found no significant difference in the total of number of ML areas picked between the two groups (W = 249.5, p = 0.725). Meaning that students who took PSTAT 134 and those who didn't showed pretty much the same overall level of interest in machine learning.


## Conclusion + Drawbacks

There a few things to consider when looking at these results. First, the groups are pretty unbalanced, with only 13 students who took PSTAT 134 compared to 36 who didn't. That small group means one or two students can skew the percentage a lot, and our tests don't have much power to pick up a real difference. Second, the "did not take PSTAT 134" group isn't all the same, since it mixes 31 students who took PSTAT 131 with 5 who took neither course, so it isnt a clean comparison. The survey also let students pick as many areas as they wanted, our six ML areas was more a judgment call, also the data is self reported interest rather than actual skill, and since students choose their own courses, we cant determine that PSTAT 134 caused any differences.



# PSTAT 131 Only vs. PSTAT 131 + 134

One issue with the last comparison is that the "did not take PSTAT 134" group also included 5 students who never took PSTAT 131. To get a cleaner comparison, we can now just look at students who took PSTAT 131 and split them into those who stopped at 131 and those who went on to take 134 as well. This way, everone has the same intro ML background, and we can see whether taking 134 on top 131 makes a difference.


## Filtering to PSTAT 131 students

```{r}
area_131 <- area_long_134 |>
  filter(str_detect(courses, fixed('PSTAT 131'))) |>
  mutate(cohort = if_else(group_134 == 'Took PSTAT 134', '131 + 134', '131 only'))
  
ml_131 <- area_131 |> 
  group_by(response_id, cohort) |>
  summarise(n_ml_areas = sum(selected), .groups = 'drop')

ml_131 |>
  count(cohort, name = 'n_students') |>
  kable(caption = 'Students by cohort')
  
```
This leaves us with 44 students, 31 who only took PSTAT 131 and 13 who took both.

## Summary

```{r}
ml_131 |>
  group_by(cohort) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_ml_areas = mean(n_ml_areas),
            median_ml_areas = median(n_ml_areas)) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = 'ML related areas selected: 131 only vs. 131 + 134')


```
Even after removing the 5 students who never took PSTAT 131, the results look almost the same as before. Students who took only 131 picked slightly more ML areas on average (4.06 vs. 3.85), and both groups had a median of 4.

## Ml Interest by Area

```{r}
area_131 |>
  group_by(cohort, area) |>
  summarise(proportion = mean(selected), .groups = 'drop') |>
  ggplot(aes(x = area, y = proportion, fill = cohort)) +
  geom_col(position = 'dodge') +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0,1)) +
  labs(title = 'ML related interests: 131 only vs. 131 + 134',
       x = NULL, y = 'Proportion of students in group', fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1))

```
From this it looks like it follows the same pattern as before, with 131 + 134 students leaning more toward data engineering (77% vs. 55%) and less toward statistical inference (46% vs. 68%). The other areas were pretty similar between the two groups.

## Testing for Differences

Finally, we can check whether any of these differences are statistically signficant.

```{r}
area_131 |>
  group_by(area) |>
  summarise(p_value = fisher.test(table(cohort, selected))$p.value) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Fisher's exact test by ML Area: 131 only vs. 131 + 134")

wilcox.test(n_ml_areas ~ cohort, data = ml_131, exact = FALSE)
```
Just like before, none of the differences were statistically signficant. Every Fisher p value was above 0.05 (the closest being dqta engineering at p = 0.198), and the Wilcox test showed no real differences in the total number of ML areas picked (W = 186, p = 0.689). So, among students who already took PSTAT 131, also taking PSTAT 134 does not seem to be linked to more interst in machine learning.
